payload.title: Wedding Veil Meaning and Why Brides Wear One
protect_keywords: why do brides wear a veil over their face
payload.audience: Couples in their 30s interested in destination weddings and luxury experiences, AUD 150k+ budget
payload.reader: An Australian bride in her 30s, planning a wedding overseas with a generous budget, who is deciding whether a veil belongs in her ceremony and wants to understand what it has meant across history and faith, who traditionally lifts it, whether to wear a family veil, and how a veil behaves on a clifftop, beach or in summer heat before she commits to one.
payload.goal: Read the free Wedded Wonderland digital magazine (primary CTA); secondary, in-context invitation to speak with a Wedded Advisor placed after the destination section.
payload.angle: Most pages answer the question with a neat story about spirits or arranged marriages and stop. We give the veil's history only as museums, the Royal Collection and faith institutions describe it: the Roman flammeum, religious veiling, Queen Victoria's lace and royal veils as their official pages record them, and the veil in Jewish, Christian and other ceremonies tied to each tradition. Then we turn to the choices a couple planning a destination wedding actually makes: who lifts the veil and when, a blusher or a veil worn back, a family heirloom carried across the world, a veil that copes with wind and heat, and the confident choice to wear none. Styles and lengths are left to our veil styles guide.
must_include: About 10 numbered sections: why brides wear veils today; the veil in ancient Rome; medieval and religious veiling; the Victorian white veil; royal veils; the veil in faith traditions; lifting the veil; blusher, wearing it back and heirloom veils; a veil for a destination wedding; choosing not to wear one

Origins, dates and meanings stated as fact only where a museum, Royal Collection Trust, Britannica, Oxford Reference or official faith source gives them; otherwise confident living practice ('Many couples...'); 'often told' at most once; no myths section
Faith customs (e.g. the Jewish bedeken) only where sourced and tied to their own tradition, written respectfully, no generalising across faiths
Royal and museum examples only as rct.uk, royal.uk, V&A or the Met describe them, cited once by link
Lifting the veil: who lifts it (partner, parent, the bride herself) as living practice; any partner of any gender, said once
Destination section as practical points: wind, heat, beach or clifftop, securing and timing (veil on for the ceremony, off for the reception); no travel or packing rules stated as fact

FAQ of 5 to 7 questions with no amounts, not repeating the styles page's FAQ (why the veil covers the face, who lifts the veil, can I wear my mother's veil, when do you take the veil off, is a veil religious)

Internal links: /style-advice/wedding-veil (styles and lengths); /expert-advice/something-old-something-new (heirloom veils); /expert-advice/wedding-traditions pillar; /style/iconic-celebrity-wedding-veils-modern-times as further reading; /magazine; /wonderland-concierge
